newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Focus - VA Stahl emphasises cost-cutting.
newsitem.headline: Focus - VA Stahl emphasises cost-cutting.

text.p: Austrian steelmaker VA Stahl AG, reporting a 45 percent drop in 1996 net profit, said on Thursday that cost-cutting was essential to offset continued price pressure in the European market.
"Costs and prices are diverging by two percent a year," VA Stahl chief executive Peter Strahammer told a news conference.
He said the firm was aiming for 500 million schillings ($42.5 million) in annual savings to add to the 3.5 billion achieved since 1993.
He reiterated that earnings in the coming year should be in line with 1996. VA Stahl has shifted its next financial year to end on March 31.

Earlier VA Stahl said its 1996 net profit fell to 1.69 billion schillings from 3.07 billion while sales dropped to 31.5 billion from 33.8 billion. The firm also announced it was cutting its dividend to 12 schillings from 13 schillings.

"The lower dividend is justified by the fall in earnings and the high level of investments in the next two years," Strahammer said. "The whole industry misjudged the situation in 1996. Last year was not a small dip but a real slump."
Spending cuts by European governments had curtailed investment in public projects at the same time as customers ran down their stocks.
"Government efforts to reach the Maastricht criteria are not good for the steel market," Strahammer noted.
He forecast the merger of German steel giants Krupp-Hoesch and Thyssen would go some way to consolidating the European steel sector but said he expected prices to remain under pressure.

VA Stahl would continue to invest heavily over the next two years but then there would be a decline in investment spending. Between 1996 and 2000 investment will total 13 billion schillings, according to VA Stahl. Spending will mainly target raising efficiency and securing VA Stahl's position in the niche automobile and home appliances industries.

VA Stahl is negotiating with Canadian-based, Austrian-owned Magna International and U.S. Chrysler to build a pressing works for the bodywork of Grand Cherokee and Voyager jeeps. Both models are assembled in Graz, southern Austria.
The firm declined to give details but sources close to the negotiations said the deal would involve an investment of two to three billion schillings.
Strahammer said VA Stahl was also eyeing a downstream expansion in eastern Europe through involvement in a joint venture.
